html:
A mosque and school in Cairo, founded by the Fatimids in 970 and finished in 972. Today it is the leading centre of Sunni learning in the world, and its head, the Grand Imam, is one of Islam's most heard voices.

It is named after Fatima al-Zahra, daughter of the prophet Muhammad. The Fatimids were Ismaili Shia, and from 988 they paid scholars to teach their doctrine there. When Saladin ended Fatimid rule he brought Egypt back to Sunni Islam and at first sidelined the mosque. Under the Mamluk sultans it revived as a Sunni school and drew students from across the Muslim world, who lodged in halls by country of origin.

During Napoleon's occupation it was a centre of the Cairo revolt of 1798. In 1961, under Gamal Abdel Nasser, the state took it over and added modern faculties such as medicine and engineering and opened it to women. Like the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, it is among the oldest working places of learning in the world.
